What Priya needs

Three tracks for , each pick backed by a number.

An editor puts a track in front of people who have never heard it. So the question is which tracks new listeners keep.

Why not sort by streams and take the top three?

Sort the sheet two ways. Left, the three with the most streams. Right, the three with the best among tracks with at least 5,000 listeners, with as the cross-check.

Top 3 by streams

    Top 3 by save rate, at least 5,000 listeners

      Streams count plays, and plays come from exposure. A track that was already on big playlists racks up streams whether or not anyone liked it. has the most streams in the catalogue; of its plays were skipped in the first 30 seconds and of the people who heard it saved it.

      Streams tell you what was pushed. Saves tell you what stuck. A playlist editor is about to give a track exposure, which is the one thing streams already measure. Rank by what happens after exposure.

      The measure: save rate

      Save rate = saves ÷ listeners.

      , saves ÷ listeners

      It answers the question an editor cares about. Of the people who heard it, how many kept it?

      Early skips are the cross-check. A track people keep is rarely one they skip in 30 seconds.

      The cut-off: at least 5,000 listeners

      Sorted by save rate alone, two small tracks come first.

      , saves from listeners
      , saves from listeners

      Those listeners probably went looking for the track, so they are existing fans. And a rate from people swings a lot: if 50 of them change their minds, it moves points.

      So the report ranks the tracks with at least 5,000 listeners, and it names the two it left out, because a reader who sorts the sheet will see them at the top and ask.

      Ask a chatbot for a "beautiful, modern dashboard" and the result lands in one of a few looks.

      Models learned design from millions of landing pages, templates and design showcases, and the most common looks win.

      A

      SaaS style

      Indigo-to-violet gradient, white cards with soft shadows, a sidebar, four tiles. The look of product pages and admin templates since about 2020. It says "product".

      B

      Editorial style

      Cream background, an italic serif on one word, small spaced capitals, numbered sections. Borrowed from newsletter platforms and brand sites that want to look considered. It says "thoughtful".

      C

      Command center

      Near-black background, neon cyan and magenta, glowing lines, frosted glass. From crypto dashboards, developer tools and film interfaces. It says "real-time".

      A model predicts the most likely design for the words in the prompt. "Beautiful", "modern" and "professional" are the words those templates were sold with, so the prompt pulls the template.

      None of the three looks is wrong for a product. All three are wrong for Priya, because the look was chosen before the question.

        When automation earns its place

        Kestrel Lane pitched the three tracks on 1 October. Every Monday the marketing team asks the same question: are they still working, or should we swap one? The export lands at 6 am. Someone used to open it, make the same chart and send the same email.

        Automate when

        • the same question comes back on a schedule
        • the data arrives in the same shape each time
        • the rule can be written down (under 9% for two weeks)

        Not worth it when

        • the question is asked once (Priya's pitch)
        • the data changes shape every time
        • setting it up costs more than the next ten manual runs

        A person decides when

        • a check fails (week 4: a track missing from the file)
        • the rule says swap, because a swap is a decision
        • the summary goes to someone, so someone reads it first

        Ask an AI to make your report "comprehensive" or "more advanced" and it will add things. Each addition makes the answer harder to find.

        PartAsk for "comprehensive" and you may getWhat your reader needs

        The right-hand column follows today's one-page checklist, Presenting results clearly. Dotted terms open a short definition.

        Over-engineering a report is over-fitting. Every extra chart, model or package fits the data a little better and the question a little worse. What it adds is noise. And noise is not noice.

        Before you add anything

        Keep everything the brief asks for. For anything else, ask two questions:

        1. Would the reader miss it if it were gone?
        2. Does it change the answer?

        If both answers are no, leave it out. Before you submit A2 or A3, take one pass through every chart, table and paragraph with these questions.

        Ask the AI for less

        Before you add or cut a chart, model, package or paragraph, tell me whether the brief asks for it. Keep everything it asks for. For anything else, tell me what it changes in the answer, and if nothing, leave it out.

        You can also ask it what a busy reader would misread on your page, then fix that yourself.
